nameStory: The 'dark fishing spider' gets its name from its dusky coloration and its family's reputation for hunting near water. However, this particular spider is something of a rebel - while its cousins hunt fish and aquatic insects at pond edges, the dark fishing spider prefers life in the trees, making it more of a 'tree-climbing fishing spider' than a true angler.
description: The dark fishing spider is a large, impressive arachnid that can span nearly 3 inches across with its legs extended. Despite its intimidating size, it's a gentle giant with a robust, chocolate-brown to grayish body marked with lighter stripes and spots. Unlike other fishing spiders that patrol water's edge, this species prefers to climb trees and hide under loose bark, making it more arboreal than aquatic.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: One of New England's largest spiders, with a body length up to 1 inch and leg span reaching nearly 3 inches - about the size of your palm when fingers are spread

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Robust, sturdy build with thick, powerful legs that feel surprisingly strong if handled - built like a spider weightlifter rather than a delicate web-spinner

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Dark brown to grayish body with lighter chevron or W-shaped markings on the abdomen, and subtle striping on the legs that creates a mottled, bark-like camouflage pattern

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Typically found on tree trunks or under loose bark rather than near water - look for them pressed flat against bark where they blend in perfectly with the texture

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Does not build webs for catching prey, instead hunts actively by ambushing insects from hiding spots on tree bark

habitat: Look for dark fishing spiders on tree trunks in wooded areas throughout New England, especially on older trees with loose or furrowed bark like oaks, maples, and pines. They prefer forest edges, wooded parks, and even residential areas with mature trees. Despite their family name, you're more likely to find them dozens of feet from the nearest water source, hiding under bark flaps or in tree crevices.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hiding spots under bark and begin active hunting. This is when you're most likely to spot them moving between trees.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible, often seen pressed against tree bark during the day. Mating occurs and females begin carrying large, spherical egg sacs.
seasonality.fall: Females may still be carrying egg sacs or guarding newly hatched spiderlings. Adults begin seeking winter shelter under loose bark.
seasonality.winter: Adults hibernate under bark or in tree crevices, remaining motionless until spring warmth triggers activity.

funFact: Dark fishing spiders are accomplished tree climbers that can run straight up a vertical tree trunk faster than you can walk, and mothers will aggressively defend their egg sacs by rearing up on their hind legs and showing their fangs - a display so dramatic it's been mistaken for a 'spider attack' by startled hikers.
confusionNotes: Often confused with wolf spiders due to their size and brown coloration, but dark fishing spiders have a more flattened body shape and are found on trees rather than on the ground. Remember: if it's big, brown, and on a tree trunk, it's likely a dark fishing spider; if it's big, brown, and running across the forest floor, think wolf spider.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'fishing spider,' this species rarely fishes and is poorly suited for aquatic life compared to its water-loving relatives. The name is somewhat misleading and reflects the family classification rather than this particular species' lifestyle - think of it as the 'landlubber' of the fishing spider family.
compareHints: Unlike the striped fishing spider and six-spotted fishing spider which are typically found near water and have more contrasting markings, the dark fishing spider has subtler coloration and lives almost exclusively on trees. It's also generally darker and more uniformly colored than its water-dwelling cousins, lacking the bold stripes or spots that give the other species their names.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's fishing spiders, the Striped Fishing Spider is distinguished by its pale brown coloration with prominent light stripes, while the Dark Fishing Spider is much darker and larger, and the Six-spotted Fishing Spider has distinctive white spots instead of stripes.
The six-spotted fishing spider is distinguished from its close relative the Dark Fishing Spider by its characteristic six light spots versus the Dark Fishing Spider's white side stripes.
Among New England's fishing spiders, the Banded Fishing Spider is distinguished by its bold, regular light bands across a dark body.
Among New England's fishing spiders, striatus has the most clearly defined striped patterns - other species like the dark fishing spider have more mottled or spotted appearances.

The white-banded fishing spider stands out from its fishing spider relatives by having the most clearly defined white bands - the dark fishing spider has more subdued, mottled markings, while the striped fishing spider shows yellowish stripes rather than bright white bands.
